ox: Correct. You blamed the stranger's personality (rude) and ignored the situation (rushing to a hospital). That is the fundamental attribution error.
Wrong. Self-serving bias is about explaining your own successes and failures. Here you judge a stranger.
Wrong. Actor-observer bias compares how you explain your own behavior versus others'. The stem only gives your judgment of another person.
Wrong. The halo effect is one good trait making you assume other good traits. No such trait is described.

p: An attribution is your explanation for why someone did something. A dispositional attribution blames traits. A situational attribution blames circumstances.
The fundamental attribution error (FAE) is the habit of overweighting traits and underweighting the situation when judging other people.

mem: FAE = judging OTHERS, overweight disposition
Underweights situation
Stronger in individualist cultures
q119.trap: Picking actor-observer bias. If only one person's behavior is judged, and it is someone else, it is FAE.
q119.plain: A kid sees a classmate drop a tray and thinks 'clumsy', never noticing the floor was wet.

ox: Correct. Success is credited to an internal cause (intelligence) and failure to an external cause (unfair test). That is self-serving bias.
Wrong. The fundamental attribution error is about how you explain other people's behavior, not your own results.
Wrong. Optimism bias is expecting good future outcomes. The stem is about explaining past results.
Wrong. Just-world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve, not a way of explaining your own grades.

p: Self-serving bias means taking credit for good outcomes and blaming outside forces for bad ones.
It protects self-esteem. Success becomes internal (my skill). Failure becomes external (bad luck, unfair test).

mem: Success = internal, failure = external
Protects self-esteem
About YOUR outcomes
q120.trap: Choosing FAE because it is more famous. FAE concerns judging others.
q120.plain: When you win the game it is because you are great. When you lose it is because the referee cheated.

ox: Correct. Reminding women of a negative stereotype creates anxiety about confirming it, which lowers performance. That is stereotype threat.
Wrong. A self-fulfilling prophecy is when an expectation changes behavior until it comes true. Here a specific reminder of a stereotype causes the drop through anxiety.
Wrong. Prejudice is a negative attitude toward a group. It is not a performance effect in the target.
Wrong. Discrimination is unfair behavior toward a group. Here no one is treating the women unfairly.

p: Stereotype threat is the worry about confirming a negative stereotype about your own group. The worry uses up mental effort.
As a result, performance drops on the exact task the stereotype is about, even if ability is the same.

mem: Target's own anxiety about a stereotype lowers performance
Triggered by a reminder of the stereotype
Thought to use working memory
q121.trap: Choosing self-fulfilling prophecy. That is about others' expectations, not the target's own fear.
q121.plain: If someone says 'kids like you always trip' right before you walk the balance beam, you get nervous and wobble.

ox: Correct. Believing victims must have deserved their fate is the just-world hypothesis, the belief that the world is fair.
Wrong. FAE is related because it blames the person, but the specific belief that outcomes are deserved marks the just-world hypothesis.
Wrong. Hindsight bias is believing you knew the outcome all along. Nothing about predicting is mentioned.
Wrong. In-group bias is favoring your own group. No group membership is described.

p: The just-world hypothesis is the belief that good things happen to good people and bad things to bad people.
It makes the world feel safe and predictable. A side effect is victim blaming, because a victim must have done something to deserve it.

mem: People get what they deserve
Leads to victim blaming
Protects belief that the world is fair
q122.trap: Choosing FAE. Look for the phrase 'deserve it' to pick just-world.
q122.plain: A kid thinks only naughty children get sick, because that way he feels safe if he is good.

ox: Wrong. A situational attribution blames circumstances outside the person. A trait explanation is the opposite.
Wrong. External causes are situational, and traits are internal. This is also not a standard label for trait explanations.
Wrong. Self-serving bias is a pattern of choosing internal causes for success and external for failure. It is not the name for every trait explanation.
Correct. A dispositional attribution places the cause inside the person: traits, abilities, effort or character.

p: An attribution is the reason you give for someone's behavior. Dispositional (internal) attributions point to the person: traits, ability, effort.
Situational (external) attributions point to circumstances, such as luck, task difficulty or other people.

mem: Dispositional = internal = traits
Situational = external = circumstances
Self-serving bias is a pattern, not an attribution type
x8B_001.trap: Mixing up the words disposition and situation, or picking self-serving bias because it sounds related.
x8B_001.plain: If your friend is late, 'he is lazy' is about him. 'Traffic was awful' is about the situation.

ox: Wrong. Low consensus and low distinctiveness with high consistency point to the person, a dispositional attribution.
Correct. Everyone acts this way (high consensus), only toward this stimulus (high distinctiveness), and reliably (high consistency). The situation is the cause.
Wrong. Low consistency means it does not happen reliably, which suggests a fluke, not a clear situational cause. Low distinctiveness also points away from the situation.
Wrong. Low consensus points to the person, and low consistency undermines any stable attribution.

p: Kelley uses three cues. Consensus: do other people act this way? Distinctiveness: does this person act this way only toward this one thing? Consistency: does it happen every time?
High-high-high points to the situation. Low consensus, low distinctiveness, high consistency points to the person.

mem: Situation = high consensus, high distinctiveness, high consistency
Person = low consensus, low distinctiveness, high consistency
Low consistency = one-time circumstance
x8B_003.trap: Mixing up which pattern means person and which means situation. Remember distinctiveness high means 'only this situation'.
x8B_003.plain: If every kid hates one scary movie, and your friend only hates that movie, and always does, the movie is the problem, not your friend.

ox: Wrong. Actor-observer bias needs a comparison of how people explain their own behavior versus others'. Only observers are judging here.
Wrong. Dissonance is discomfort from your own inconsistent beliefs and actions. Observers judging someone else's essay are not in that situation.
Wrong. A self-fulfilling prophecy needs an expectation to change someone's actual behavior. Nothing of that kind is shown.
Correct. Observers inferred an attitude matching the essay even though it was forced by a coin flip. That is correspondence bias, another name for the FAE.

p: Correspondence bias is inferring that someone's behavior matches their inner attitude, even when the situation forced that behavior.
It is the same idea as the fundamental attribution error. The coin flip is the obvious situational cause that observers ignore.

mem: Correspondence bias = FAE
Occurs even when constraints are obvious
Classic essay-assignment design
x8B_006.trap: Choosing actor-observer bias. No self-versus-other comparison exists in this design.
x8B_006.plain: An actor plays a villain in a movie, and a kid decides the actor is truly mean.

ox: Wrong. Reducing mental effort is the job of heuristics and stereotypes. Self-serving bias is motivated by feelings about the self.
Correct. Taking credit for success and deflecting blame for failure protects and boosts self-esteem.
Wrong. The bias distorts self-assessment, so it lowers accuracy.
Wrong. That fits group-serving bias, which favors the in-group. Self-serving bias is about the individual.

p: Self-serving bias is motivated reasoning. This means the brain bends explanations to feel good.
Crediting yourself for wins and blaming circumstances for losses keeps your self-worth up, even though it is less accurate.

mem: Function = protect and enhance self-esteem
Costs accuracy
Group version = group-serving bias
x8B_009.plain: It is like a kid who says 'I scored the goal' but 'the wind made me miss'. It protects his pride.

ox: Wrong. Stereotype threat affects performance of members of a stereotyped group. It does not explain observers judging a victim.
Wrong. Self-serving bias is about explaining your own successes and failures. The participants' own outcomes are not involved.
Wrong. The halo effect is one good trait spreading to other traits. It has nothing to do with fairness beliefs.
Correct. When justice cannot be restored, devaluing the victim makes the outcome seem deserved, protecting the belief that the world is fair.

p: People with a strong just-world belief expect good people to be rewarded and bad people punished.
An unpunished crime against an innocent person threatens that belief. Lowering your opinion of the victim fixes the threat in your mind.

mem: Just-world belief -> blame or devalue victims
Strongest when justice cannot be restored
It restores a sense of fairness
x8B_011.trap: Choosing self-serving bias just because a bias is named. Ask whose outcome is being explained.
x8B_011.plain: If a good kid gets hurt and no one is blamed, a child who believes in fairness decides the kid must have been not so good.

ox: Wrong. No culture uses traits only. A stronger trait emphasis is typical of individualist cultures.
Wrong. Self-serving bias tends to be weaker, not stronger, in collectivist samples, because modesty and group harmony are valued.
Wrong. Collectivist cultures emphasize roles and relationships, so they do not ignore them.
Correct. Collectivist cultures stress interdependence, so people consider context and roles, and show a weaker FAE.

p: Individualist cultures (such as the US) value the independent self. People there lean toward trait explanations.
Collectivist cultures (such as many East Asian societies) value group ties and roles. People there more often consider the situation.

mem: Individualist -> dispositional, stronger FAE
Collectivist -> situational, weaker FAE
Self-serving bias is also weaker in collectivist cultures
x8B_012.trap: Picking 'exclusively' options. Absolute words are rarely correct on the MCAT.
x8B_012.plain: One family says 'what is wrong with him?' Another says 'what happened around him?'

ox: Wrong. If the bias were fixed, coverage would look the same everywhere. The cross-cultural difference argues against it.
Wrong. Both sets of papers explained someone else's behavior. Actor-observer bias needs a self-versus-other comparison.
Correct. The emphasis on personality versus circumstances differed by culture, so the bias is shaped by culture.
Wrong. Stereotype threat is about performance under a stereotype, not newspaper explanations of crimes.

p: If a bias were universal and fixed in the same way, results should look the same in every culture.
Here American papers stressed the killer's personality and Chinese-language papers stressed circumstances. Cultural background changes how strong the FAE is.

mem: Individualist -> dispositional focus
Collectivist -> situational focus
Variation across cultures means the bias is not fixed
x8B_013.trap: Choosing actor-observer bias because it also sounds like attribution. No one explained their own behavior.
x8B_013.plain: Two schools describe the same playground fight. One blames the bully, the other blames what led up to it.

ox: Wrong. Individual prejudice is a person's negative attitude. The stem says the company holds none.
Wrong. Stereotype threat is anxiety that lowers performance after a stereotype reminder. No test performance is described.
Wrong. A self-fulfilling prophecy needs an expectation that changes behavior. No expectation is described.
Correct. A neutral-looking policy carries past exclusion forward and produces unequal outcomes, with no individual prejudice needed.

p: Discrimination is unequal treatment or outcomes for a group. Institutional discrimination comes from policies and rules, not from individual attitudes.
A rule that seems neutral can still shut a group out if it depends on past exclusion.

mem: Prejudice = attitude
Discrimination = behavior or outcome
Institutional = built into policies
Can happen with no bad intent
x8B_017.trap: Picking individual prejudice. The stem rules it out by saying the company holds no negative views.
x8B_017.plain: A club says 'only people whose parents were members may join'. Nobody is mean, but the same people always get in.

ox: Wrong. Liking the test is not a measure of working memory. It shows only an attitude.
Wrong. This shows the effect is specific to stereotyped groups. It says nothing about how it works.
Wrong. Time on a question does not directly measure working memory capacity.
Correct. A mediator that changes with the condition and statistically explains the score drop supports the mechanism.

concept.t: Testing a mechanism with a mediator
p: To show how an effect works, you need a mediator. A mediator is a middle step that the manipulation changes and that explains the result.
Here, threat lowers working memory span, and that lower span explains the lower scores.

mem: Mediator = the step that explains how
The manipulation must change it
It must account for the outcome statistically
x8B_022.trap: Choosing results that only show the effect exists. Showing it exists is different from showing how.
x8B_022.plain: If a kid is slow because his backpack is heavy, you show it by weighing the bag and seeing that weight explains the slowness.

ox: Wrong. Randomization does not control whether the deception is discovered.
Correct. Random assignment makes the groups equal on average in ability, so a gain difference is due to the teacher expectation.
Wrong. Representativeness comes from random sampling, not random assignment. That affects external validity.
Wrong. The unlabeled students are the control group. Random assignment is what makes that comparison fair.

p: Random assignment means chance decides who gets which condition. This makes the groups similar on average in ability and motivation.
So a later difference can be blamed on the manipulation. This supports causal claims (internal validity).

mem: Random assignment -> internal validity -> cause and effect
Random sampling -> external validity -> generalizing
Control group still needed
x8B_025.trap: Confusing random assignment with random sampling.
x8B_025.plain: Draw names from a hat to decide who gets the sticker, so the sticker kids are not just the ones who were already best.

ox: Correct. Goals both groups wanted but could only reach together (fixing the water supply) reduced hostility. These are superordinate goals.
Wrong. Simple contact had already failed to reduce hostility during the competition. Contact helps only under conditions like shared goals.
Wrong. Deindividuation is losing a sense of individual identity in a group, which increases antisocial behavior.
Wrong. Social loafing is people working less in a group. The campers worked together.

p: A superordinate goal is a goal that both groups want and neither can reach alone. This forces cooperation.
In the Robbers Cave study, competition caused hostility. Cooperating on shared problems, like the water supply, reduced it.

mem: Robbers Cave: competition -> hostility
Superordinate goals reduce conflict
Contact alone is not enough
x8B_031.trap: Picking mere contact. Shared meals did not help without a common goal.
x8B_031.plain: Two rival teams have to carry one heavy couch together, and suddenly they are one team.

ox: Correct. Everyone saw the same lecture, so only the label differed. The label changed how students acted (fewer questions), not just their private ratings.
The stem says all students saw the same lecture. Choosing this ignores that detail and invents a flaw in the design.
Self-serving bias means explaining your OWN successes and failures in a flattering way. Students here were judging another person, so it does not fit.
Warm and cold are actually central traits: they strongly shape the whole impression. Calling them peripheral misses how large the effect was.

p: A first impression is the quick picture you form of a person. It can do more than color your opinion. It can change how you act toward that person.

In this study, the label 'cold' made students engage less. A target who gets less engagement may then act more coldly. This is the start of a self-fulfilling prophecy (an expectation that causes itself to come true).

mem: Warm and cold are central traits (they shape the whole impression).
Impressions can change behavior toward the target.
Same stimulus plus different label equals the label caused the difference.
x8B_037.sc: Read the stem for what is held constant. Only the label varied, so the label is the cause.
x8B_037.trap: Do not pick 'different lecture' when the stem says all saw the same lecture.
x8B_037.plain: If a teacher is called mean before you meet her, you may not raise your hand. Then she seems mean because nobody talks to her.

ox: The results show MORE reliance on the speaker's fidgeting (a trait-like cue), not less. A purely situational model predicts the opposite.
Correct. People first quickly infer a trait from behavior, then effortfully adjust for the situation. Memorizing a number uses up mental effort, so the adjustment step is skipped.
Just-world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve. Nobody is judging fairness of an outcome here.
Social facilitation is how an audience changes your performance on a task. The participants were judging someone else, not performing in front of others.

p: Attribution means explaining why someone acted a certain way. Step 1 is automatic: we assume the behavior shows the person's trait. Step 2 takes effort: we correct for the situation.
Cognitive load means your mind is busy. When busy, you do step 1 only. So the stressful topic (the situation) gets ignored and the fidgeting is blamed on the person's anxious nature.

mem: Step 1: automatic trait inference.
Step 2: effortful situational correction.
Cognitive load blocks step 2, so more dispositional attributions.
x8B_041.sc: Distracted or busy perceiver means more dispositional (trait) blame.
x8B_041.trap: Do not confuse this with fundamental attribution error alone. The key is the distraction removing the correction step.
x8B_041.plain: You jump to 'she is just a nervous person.' With a free mind you remember 'oh, the topic is scary.' A busy mind skips that second thought.

ox: Rapid presentation in one session keeps the first items active in memory and shapes how later items are read. That favors primacy.
If you are distracted during the later information, you take in less of it, so it has less impact. That favors primacy, not recency.
Correct. A long delay lets the first information fade. Judging right after the second set means the most recent information is freshest, so recency wins.
Vivid early information is memorable and strong. That pushes toward primacy, the usual result.

p: Primacy effect means first information has the most impact. Recency effect means the latest information has the most impact.
Primacy wins when early information frames how we read later information. Recency wins when the early information has faded and the latest is fresh in memory.

mem: Primacy is the default in impression formation.
Recency needs a delay after the first info and a judgment soon after the last.
Distraction during later info weakens it.
x8B_045.trap: Do not pick distraction. Distraction on later information weakens recency.
x8B_045.plain: Think of a movie: the opening makes a strong impression, but if you answer a survey right after a long gap and a strong ending, the ending dominates.

ox: Self-serving bias is about explaining your OWN outcomes (credit for success, blame for failure). Here the observer judges an out-group member.
Correct. Ultimate attribution error: for out-group members, good acts are explained away as luck or exceptions, and bad acts are blamed on their character.
False consensus effect is overestimating how many others share your views. No such estimate is made here.
Recency effect is about the order of information. No order is described.

p: Attribution means explaining behavior. The ultimate attribution error applies a bias to whole groups. For a disliked out-group, bad acts are blamed on character, and good acts are blamed on luck or special circumstances.
This lets a prejudiced person keep their belief even when they see evidence against it.

mem: Out-group negative equals dispositional.
Out-group positive equals luck, exception, or situation.
It is a group-level attribution bias.
x8B_051.trap: Self-serving bias sounds similar, but it is about the self, not an out-group.
x8B_051.plain: If your rival team wins, it was luck. If your own team wins, it was skill.

ox: The same faces were used in both groups, so the faces cannot be objectively different. Only the clip differed.
One short session cannot show permanent change. The stem shows only a brief effect on ratings.
Correct. Random assignment means the clip (and the mood it created) is the likely cause of the more hostile ratings. Emotional state can bias how we read social cues.
Stereotype threat is worry about confirming a negative stereotype, which hurts performance. It is not about rating faces and no stereotype is mentioned.

p: Social perception is how we read other people. Ambiguous faces can be read as friendly or hostile. A scared mood pushes people to read them as hostile.
Random assignment (chance decides who is in which group) makes the groups equal except for the clip. So the difference in ratings is probably caused by the clip.

mem: Random assignment supports causal conclusions.
Mood and emotion can bias social perception.
Do not claim permanent effects from one session.
x8B_055.plain: If you just watched a horror movie, a stranger in the hallway looks more threatening.

ox: Confirmation bias is searching for or favoring evidence that supports what you already believe. It is not seeing a link that is not there.
Base-rate fallacy is ignoring how common something is overall when judging a specific case. It does not describe seeing a false link.
Correct. Illusory correlation is seeing a relationship between two variables when none exists. Rare things that appear together stand out, so we think they are linked.
Belief perseverance is holding on to a belief after the evidence for it has been discredited.

p: A correlation is a link between two things. An illusory correlation is a link you think you see but is not real.
It is most likely when two rare or distinctive things happen together, like a small group and an unusual behavior. Those pairs are memorable, so they seem to go together.

mem: Illusory correlation: perceiving a link that does not exist.
Rare plus rare pairings are memorable.
It can feed stereotypes.
x8B_056.trap: Confirmation bias maintains beliefs but does not create the perceived link.
x8B_056.plain: You remember the one time a black cat crossed your path and you tripped, and forget the many times nothing happened.

ox: The stem says undesirable behavior was in the same proportion in both groups. So Group B did not act worse per member.
Correct. Group B is the smaller group and undesirable acts are rare. Two rare things together stand out in memory, so people think they go together.
Out-group homogeneity is seeing out-group members as all alike. No in-group or out-group was set up, and the effect is about Group B ratings.
Recency effect is about order of information. Order was not changed.

p: An illusory correlation is a false link between two things. Here the two things are 'small group' and 'bad behavior'.
Both are rare in the statements, so each pairing is vivid. People remember those pairings and overestimate how often the small group acted badly.

mem: Rare group plus rare behavior creates a false link.
Same proportions means no real difference.
Minority groups are often the victims.
x8B_057.sc: When proportions are equal but one group is judged worse, think illusory correlation.
x8B_057.trap: Do not assume a real difference; the design held the proportion equal.
x8B_057.plain: In a class, the one new kid who gets in trouble is remembered. A big group's same trouble is not.

ox: Stereotype threat is the pressure a stereotyped person feels to confirm a negative stereotype. It affects the target's performance, not how an observer keeps a stereotype.
Superordinate goals are shared goals that need cooperation, used to reduce group conflict. Nothing like that happens here.
A self-fulfilling prophecy is when an expectation changes the target's behavior so it comes true. Here the observer just labels her an exception.
Correct. Subtyping places a person who does not fit the stereotype into a special subgroup ('the exception') so the stereotype stays unchanged.

p: A stereotype is a fixed belief about a group. Subtyping is when you meet someone who does not fit, and you put them in a separate small category instead of changing your belief.
This is why meeting one counterexample often fails to change stereotypes. Change works better when many typical group members disprove the stereotype.

mem: Subtyping: 'the exception that proves the rule.'
It protects stereotypes from disconfirming evidence.
Spread-out counterexamples change stereotypes more.
x8B_059.trap: Self-fulfilling prophecy needs the target's behavior to change, which does not happen here.
x8B_059.plain: Someone thinks all cats are mean, then meets a friendly cat and says 'she is a special cat.' The belief about cats stays.

ox: Correct. The argument says stereotypes justify unequal access to wealth and status, which is about power, prestige, and class (the structure of society).
Cognitive limitations (mental shortcuts) are an individual-level cause of stereotypes. The sociologist is talking about group interests instead.
Random personality variation is an individual-level idea. The argument is about social structure, not personality.
Biological threat detection is an evolved-fear idea. The argument is about social hierarchy.

p: Sociologists with a conflict view say groups compete for resources. The group in power spreads beliefs that make its advantage seem fair.
Prejudice then keeps the hierarchy in place. Sources are power (ability to control others), prestige (social respect), and class (economic position).

mem: Power, prestige, class: structural sources of prejudice.
Conflict theory: dominant groups benefit from stereotypes.
Cognitive explanations are individual-level.
x8B_063.trap: Do not pick individual-level answers when the stem talks about groups and wealth.
x8B_063.plain: If one kid owns all the toys, he may say the others are too clumsy to play with them. The story protects his advantage.

ox: Public stigma is the negative attitude of other people. Here the man himself believes he is weak, so it is internalized.
Stereotype lift is a performance boost from comparing your group to a negatively stereotyped group. It does not apply.
Courtesy stigma happens to people connected to someone stigmatized, like family members. He is the diagnosed person himself.
Correct. Self-stigma is when a person absorbs society's negative views about their condition and applies them to themselves, lowering self-esteem and help seeking.

p: Stigma is a mark of shame attached to a group or condition. Public stigma comes from others. Self-stigma comes from yourself after you accept those views.
Courtesy stigma, also called associative, is aimed at people linked to a stigmatized person. Self-stigma can make people avoid help.

mem: Public stigma: others' attitudes.
Self-stigma: internalized.
Courtesy stigma: people associated with the person.
x8B_065.trap: Public stigma is tempting, but the key detail is that the man believes it himself.
x8B_065.plain: If everyone calls a kid lazy, he may start to think he really is lazy and quit trying.

ox: Correlation alone does not prove cause. A third factor, like symptom severity, could be responsible.
Correct. The researcher only measured both things, so the justified claim is an association.
Reverse causation is also not proven. Missing sessions causing beliefs is just as unsupported.
The data show an association, so claiming stigma has no effect contradicts the finding.

p: A correlation means two things tend to go together. Causation means one makes the other happen.
To show cause, researchers must manipulate one variable and randomly assign people. Measuring both only shows association. Also consider direction (which causes which) and third variables.

mem: Correlation does not equal causation.
Look for reverse causation.
Look for third variables.
x8B_067.sc: With no manipulation, choose the answer that says 'associated with'.
x8B_067.trap: Choosing the causal answer is the classic overreach.
x8B_067.plain: Ice cream sales and sunburns rise together, but ice cream does not cause sunburn. Summer does.

ox: Correct. Explicit attitudes are what you consciously report. Implicit attitudes are automatic. They can disagree.
Self-report scales measure explicit (conscious) attitudes, not implicit ones.
Implicit bias can exist without awareness, so the person need not be lying. Assuming deception is the tempting trap.
The reaction-time test did detect strong automatic bias here, so this contradicts the stem.

p: Explicit attitudes are beliefs you know you have and can report. Implicit attitudes are automatic associations, often outside awareness.
Reaction-time tests, such as the Implicit Association Test (IAT), measure how fast you pair groups with good or bad words. Faster pairing means stronger association.

mem: Explicit equals self-report.
Implicit equals indirect measures like reaction time.
They can diverge without lying.
x8B_069.trap: Do not assume dishonesty when the two measures disagree.
x8B_069.plain: You may sincerely say you like all foods but your hand still reaches away from broccoli without thinking.

ox: Overt discrimination is open and obvious. This person only avoids when an excuse is available.
Institutional discrimination comes from policies and practices of organizations, not an individual's avoidance.
Cultural relativism is understanding a culture on its own terms. It is not a form of bias.
Correct. Aversive racism: people who sincerely hold equal values still have hidden negative feelings, which show up only when they can blame a nonracial reason.

p: Aversive racism is a subtle form of prejudice. The person sincerely thinks they are fair, but has unadmitted negative feelings.
The bias shows only when behavior can be explained by something else, like 'I was busy.' This protects their self-image as a fair person.

mem: Aversive racism: egalitarian belief plus hidden bias.
Appears in ambiguous situations with an excuse.
Overt discrimination does not need an excuse.
x8B_070.trap: Overt discrimination is tempting, but the dependence on excuses points to aversive racism.
x8B_070.plain: A kid who says he is kind to everyone but skips one classmate only when he can claim he had no time.

ox: This result shows a non-disadvantaged group (white male math majors) was affected, so the claim is false.
The groups were not shown to differ in true ability. The effect came from the situation.
The test was a math test. Nothing limits stereotype threat to verbal tests.
Correct. Stereotype threat can hit any group when a relevant stereotype makes an unfavorable comparison, even high-status groups.

p: Stereotype threat is worry about confirming a negative stereotype about your group. That worry uses up mental resources and lowers performance.
Here, white men were compared with Asian students, a group stereotyped as better at math. The threat was in the situation, not in their ability.

mem: Stereotype threat is situational.
It can affect any group.
It reduces performance via anxiety.
x8B_076.trap: Do not assume it only applies to historically disadvantaged groups.
x8B_076.plain: Imagine taking a test while being told you are being compared with the school's top team. Nerves make you do worse.

ox: Correct. Methodological relativism means understanding a practice in context before judging. It does not claim every practice is morally acceptable, which answers the critique directly.
Ethnocentrism means judging other cultures by your own standards. Rejecting extreme relativism does not require this.
Saying harmful practices do not exist ignores the critique instead of answering it.
Relativism is about understanding, not adopting another culture's practices.

p: Cultural relativism means judging a practice within its own culture's context. Ethnocentrism means judging all cultures by your own standards.
Methodological relativism is a research stance: first understand. Moral relativism says no practice can ever be judged wrong. They are different.

mem: Cultural relativism: understand in context.
Ethnocentrism: own culture as the standard.
Methodological relativism is not moral relativism.
x8B_080.trap: Do not mix up understanding a practice with approving it.
x8B_080.plain: A good doctor first asks about symptoms before giving a diagnosis. Understanding comes before judging.

ox: That supports an informational account: actors have more knowledge of their own history. It does not test salience.
Liking is a motivational factor, not about what is visually prominent.
Correct. When actors saw themselves from an observer's viewpoint, their attributions became more dispositional. Changing what is visually salient changed attributions.
That is self-serving bias, where we blame outside causes for our own failures.

p: Actor-observer bias is when we blame the situation for our own behavior but blame personality for others' behavior.
The salience account says what is most visible shapes the explanation. Actors see the situation. Observers see the actor. Changing the viewpoint changes the explanation.

mem: Actors: situational. Observers: dispositional.
Salience account: what you see most becomes the cause.
Informational account: actors know own history.
x8B_087.trap: Do not confuse salience with informational or self-serving explanations.
x8B_087.plain: When you are driving you notice the traffic. When you watch someone else drive, you notice the driver.

ox: Wrong. Roles were assigned at random, so the writers did not know more overall. Trap: believing the result is real because it looks real.

Correct. Writers pick questions from things they already know, which is an unfair built-in advantage. Observers ignored that role and blamed the writers' intelligence instead. That is the fundamental attribution error.
Wrong. Blaming question difficulty is a situational explanation, which is the opposite of the error. The error is ignoring the situation. Trap: mixing up which direction the error goes.
Wrong. Answerers blaming bad luck would be self-serving bias, which is about explaining your own failures. The stem is about how observers judged others.

p: Attribution means explaining why someone acted a certain way. The FAE is our habit of explaining other people's behavior by their personality or ability (dispositional) and ignoring the situation (situational) around them.
Here, the writer role gave an unfair edge. Observers saw only the outcome and credited the writers' intelligence.

mem: FAE = overweight disposition, underweight situation, when judging OTHERS.
Self-serving bias = taking credit for success, blaming situation for your own failure.
Random assignment means groups should not differ in real ability.
x8B_089.trap: Do not call any attribution error FAE. It must be observers ignoring a situational cause, such as a role advantage.
x8B_089.plain: Imagine one kid picks the game and always wins because he knows its rules. You say he is just smarter, forgetting he picked the game.

ox: Wrong. Just-world thinking says people get what they deserve, so it predicts more blame of victims in general. It does not depend on similarity. Trap: any victim blaming looks like just-world.
Wrong. Out-group homogeneity is seeing out-group members as all alike. No sameness judgment is measured here.
Wrong. Stereotype threat is worry about confirming a negative stereotype and hurting your own performance. Jurors are not being tested.
Correct. Blaming a victim who is like you would suggest you could be blamed too. So you blame less to protect yourself. That is defensive attribution.

p: Defensive attribution is a way of assigning blame that protects you from feeling vulnerable. When someone similar to you suffers, you blame the situation or bad luck. That way it feels less likely to happen to you.
When the victim is different from you, blaming them is easier because it does not threaten you.

mem: Defensive attribution: similar victim gives less blame; dissimilar victim gives more blame.
Just-world hypothesis: blame victims generally, believing the world is fair.
Goal of defensive attribution is protecting the self.
x8B_091.trap: The word similar is the clue. Just-world does not care about similarity.
x8B_091.plain: If a kid just like you trips on the playground, you say the ground was bumpy. If you blame the kid, then you might be to blame next time too.

ox: Wrong. Both groups saw the same animation, so eyesight was equal. The difference was how they explained it. Trap: picking a perception answer when the stem describes interpretation.
Correct. Chinese participants (more holistic, collectivist) focused on the group and context as causes. Americans (more individualist) focused on the fish's own choice.
Wrong. Stereotype threat needs a negative stereotype about performance. None is present.
Wrong. Primacy effect means early information is remembered better. Order was not manipulated.

p: Individualist cultures stress the person as a separate unit, so people tend to explain behavior by inner traits. Collectivist cultures stress groups and relationships, so people notice context more.
This is why the fundamental attribution error tends to be weaker in collectivist cultures.

mem: Individualist (US, Western Europe): dispositional explanations.
Collectivist (East Asia): more attention to context.
Same stimulus, different interpretation means culture shapes thinking.
x8B_094.trap: Do not choose a perception or memory effect when both groups saw the identical display.
x8B_094.plain: One kid says the runner ran because he wanted to. Another kid says the team was chasing him. Same race, different focus.

ox: Wrong. The screen does not change how anyone plays. It only changes what judges know. Trap: crediting the people instead of the procedure.
Correct. Same sound, same pool, but a different result once gender was hidden. So knowing the gender must have influenced earlier decisions.
Wrong. Stereotype threat would affect performance of the stereotyped group, and men are not the stereotyped group here. Nothing in the stem shows it.
Wrong. The stem says the applicant pool was unchanged. Fewer women applying would also not raise the share advancing.

p: Blind evaluation hides identity details so a judge must rely only on performance. If the results change, the hidden detail was affecting the judgment.
This is a simple way to detect bias. The only thing that changed was what the judges knew.

mem: Result changes when identity is hidden means identity biased the judgment.
Screens change the judge's knowledge, not the performer's skill.
Check what stayed constant, here the applicant pool.
x8B_099.trap: The stem rules out pool change, so pick the answer about the evaluators.
x8B_099.plain: If a teacher grades with names covered and grades change, the names were affecting the grades.

ox: Wrong. Pain scores were already identical, so reporting rates do not explain the treatment gap.
Correct. If doctors with higher implicit bias show bigger gaps, the gap follows the proposed cause. That supports bias.
Wrong. Insurance is a structural confound, an alternative explanation. It weakens the bias claim rather than supporting it.
Wrong. Staff diversity does not measure any link between a provider's bias and treatment. It tests nothing about the cause.

concept.t: Linking a cause to an outcome
p: To show bias causes a gap, you need evidence that the amount of bias goes with the size of the gap. This is a dose-response link.
A confound is a different factor, like insurance, that could explain the result instead.

mem: Best evidence for a cause: more of the cause gives more of the effect.
A confound is an outside factor that offers a different explanation.
Implicit bias is automatic and unconscious.
x8B_100.trap: Pick the finding that ties the bias measure to the outcome, not one that just describes the setting.
x8B_100.plain: If kids who ate more candy got more cavities, candy is a likely cause. Just seeing both in one town proves little.

ox: Wrong. Pity goes with warm but low-competence groups, such as elderly people in this model.
Wrong. Contempt goes with groups seen as low in both warmth and competence.
Wrong. Admiration goes with groups seen as high in both. This group is low in warmth.
Correct. High competence with low warmth gives envy. The group is seen as capable but cold or a threat.

p: This model sorts groups on two traits: warmth (friendly, trustworthy) and competence (capable). The mix predicts the emotion people feel toward the group.
High on both gives admiration. Low on both gives contempt. Warm but not competent gives pity. Competent but cold gives envy.

mem: High warmth, high competence: admiration.
High warmth, low competence: pity.
Low warmth, high competence: envy.
Low warmth, low competence: contempt.
x8B_102.trap: Do not swap pity and envy. Match the missing trait: missing competence is pity, missing warmth is envy.
x8B_102.plain: A kid who is very good at everything but not nice to anyone makes others jealous, not sorry for him.

ox: Wrong. Out-group homogeneity is thinking out-group members are all alike. It says nothing about judging in-group members harshly.
Wrong. Ultimate attribution error is explaining out-group behavior (good acts as luck, bad acts as traits). It is not about in-group deviants.
Wrong. Group polarization is when group discussion makes opinions more extreme. No discussion is involved.
Correct. The black sheep effect is praising likable in-group members but punishing unlikable ones more than out-group members, to protect the group's image.

p: People want their own group to look good. A likable member supports that image, so they are praised. An unlikable member harms it, so they are judged more harshly than an out-group person doing the same thing.
This fits social identity theory, which says we get self-esteem from our group.

mem: Black sheep effect: good in-group member loved, bad in-group member harshly punished.
Ultimate attribution error: about explaining out-group behavior.
Rooted in social identity theory.
x8B_107.trap: Look for in-group members judged more harshly. Other options deal with out-groups or discussion.
x8B_107.plain: If your own team's player cheats, you are angrier than if the other team's player cheats, because he makes your team look bad.

ox: Wrong. Pure self-interest would pick the option giving their group the most points. They gave up points.
Wrong. Cultural relativism means judging a culture by its own standards. It has nothing to do with point allocation.
Wrong. Fairness would favor equal splits. Choosing a bigger margin is not fair.
Correct. Choosing the largest gap, even at a cost to their own group, shows people care about being ahead of the other group, not just about their own total.

p: Tajfel's studies split people into trivial groups and let them hand out points. Many chose to maximize the difference between groups, even losing points.
Social identity theory explains this: we gain self-esteem by seeing our group as better, called positive distinctiveness.

mem: Tajfel's minimal group studies show favoritism even with meaningless groups.
Social identity theory: self-esteem from group status.
Favoritism often means relative, not absolute, advantage.
x8B_108.trap: Do not choose self-interest. The choice costs the in-group points.
x8B_108.plain: A kid would rather win 5 to 2 than tie 8 to 8, because beating the other team matters most.

ox: Wrong. Mistakes under time pressure do not show conscious hostility. Such bias appears even in people without it.
Correct. Fast decisions reveal automatic stereotype associations, linking Black targets with danger, which cause the extra errors.
Wrong. The objects were controlled, so race of target was the only difference. Trap: blaming the stimuli.
Wrong. More time allows controlled thinking to correct automatic responses, so errors would likely drop.

p: Implicit bias is an automatic, unconscious association between a group and a trait. It shows up most when people must decide quickly and cannot think carefully.
Controlled processing is slow, deliberate thinking. It can correct automatic responses if there is time.

mem: Implicit biases act automatically and unconsciously.
Time pressure increases their influence.
Implicit does not mean the person consciously dislikes the group.
x8B_116.trap: Do not read errors as proof of conscious prejudice or of a flawed stimulus.
x8B_116.plain: If you have to grab something in one second, you grab by habit. With more time, you think and fix your mistake.

ox: Wrong. Scores dropped under threat, so the effect is present. Trap: overgeneralizing from a null mediator.
Wrong. One study with self-report cannot prove anxiety never matters. Self-reports can also miss anxiety.
Correct. A mediator should differ between conditions and explain the effect. Anxiety did not differ, so it does not seem to explain it here.
Wrong. Scores differed between conditions, so the manipulation had an effect.

p: A mediator is the middle step that explains how a cause produces an effect. If threat lowers scores through anxiety, anxiety should be higher under threat.
Here, it was not. So anxiety is probably not the mechanism in this study. Something else, such as reduced working memory, might be.

mem: Mediator = how or why an effect happens.
If the mediator does not change, it does not explain the effect.
One null result does not prove irrelevance everywhere.
x8B_119.trap: Avoid extreme answers like proven irrelevant in every case.
x8B_119.plain: If rain makes you late, the middle step might be traffic. If traffic was the same on rainy and sunny days, traffic is not the reason.

ox: Wrong. The FAE is about explaining behavior by traits instead of situations. This coach is choosing which trait to notice.
Wrong. Out-group homogeneity needs comparison between in-group and out-group. None is described.
Wrong. Stereotype threat harms performance when a stereotype is activated. Nobody's performance is described.
Correct. A self-schema is an organized belief about yourself. The coach values toughness, so toughness becomes the lens for judging everyone.

p: A schema is a mental framework that organizes information. A self-schema is a framework about yourself, such as I am tough.
Traits central to your self-schema become the traits you notice most in other people.

mem: Self-schema = organized beliefs about the self.
Central self-traits shape how we judge others.
FAE is about trait versus situation, a different idea.
x8B_123.trap: Do not pick the FAE just because it is familiar. Check what the stem actually describes.
x8B_123.plain: If you love soccer, you notice who is good at soccer and hardly notice who draws well.
